blocks.text: A plain binary search tree can degrade badly: inserting sorted or nearly sorted data produces a tree that resembles a linked list, turning every O(log n) operation into O(n). An AVL tree solves this by enforcing a strict balance invariant after every insertion and deletion, guaranteeing O(log n) height, and therefore O(log n) search, insert, and delete, always, regardless of insertion order.

blocks.caption: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 in order into a plain BST produces a fully skewed, linked-list-like tree; an AVL tree rebalances to keep height logarithmic.

blocks.text: This topic assumes you already understand plain BST insert and search. If not, review the general BST introduction first, this topic focuses specifically on what makes AVL trees SELF BALANCING.

Every node in an AVL tree maintains a balance factor: the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. The AVL invariant requires this balance factor to always be -1, 0, or +1 for EVERY node in the tree. Whenever an insertion or deletion would push a node's balance factor outside this range, a rotation is performed to restore it.

Each node typically stores its own height directly (updated after every structural change) so the balance factor is an O(1) lookup, height of left child minus height of right child, rather than something that needs to be recomputed by walking the subtree every time it is checked.
When a node's balance factor goes out of range, exactly one of four cases applies, identified by which side is too tall and, within that side, which of ITS children is too tall.

items: Left Left case: the left subtree is too tall, and the imbalance is further left within it. Fixed with a single RIGHT rotation.
Right Right case: the right subtree is too tall, and the imbalance is further right within it. Fixed with a single LEFT rotation, the mirror image of Left Left.

Left Right case: the left subtree is too tall, but the imbalance is to the RIGHT within it. Fixed with a LEFT rotation on the left child first, converting it into a Left Left shape, then a RIGHT rotation on the node itself.
Right Left case: the mirror of Left Right, a RIGHT rotation on the right child first, then a LEFT rotation on the node itself.

content.title: 3. The Left Left Case in Detail

blocks.caption: Before: z is unbalanced with y as its left child and x as y's left child. After a single right rotation, y becomes the new subtree root, with x as its left child and z as its right child.
blocks.alt: The Left Left Case in Detail

blocks.text: Walking through the pointer reassignment for a single right rotation on node z (with left child y, and y's left child x): y becomes the new root of this subtree. z becomes y's RIGHT child. y's original right child (if any) becomes z's new LEFT child, since it was greater than y but less than z, that ordering must be preserved. Finally, both z and y have their stored heights recomputed, since their subtrees changed.

The insert function follows the standard recursive BST insert pattern, walking down to find the correct empty spot, then, on the way back UP the call stack, updates each ancestor's height and checks its balance factor, applying the correct rotation the moment any node is found out of balance.

Because the balance invariant guarantees height is always O(log n), search, insert, and delete are all O(log n) guaranteed, with no worst case degradation, directly contrasting with a plain BST's O(n) worst case on adversarial insertion orders like sorted data.

Each insertion performs at most a constant number of rotations (at most one Left Left/Right Right style single rotation OR one Left Right/Right Left style double rotation, applied once at the first unbalanced ancestor found while unwinding the recursion), so a rotation adds only O(1) extra work per level, keeping the total insert cost at O(log n).

content.title: 6. AVL Trees vs Red Black Trees

blocks.content: {"headers":["","AVL Tree","Red Black Tree"],"rows":[["Balance strictness","Very strict, balance factor within 1","Looser, height can be up to about twice the minimum"],["Lookup speed","Faster, tighter height bound","Slightly slower, marginally taller trees"],["Insert/delete cost","More rotations on average","Fewer rotations, cheaper to keep balanced"],["Typical usage","Lookup heavy workloads","Write heavy workloads, e.g. most standard library map implementations"]]}

blocks.text: This tradeoff is why AVL trees are preferred when reads vastly outnumber writes, while Red Black trees, being cheaper to rebalance, are the more common choice for general purpose ordered map and set implementations in standard libraries, where inserts and deletes happen frequently alongside lookups.

Forgetting to update a node's height after a rotation: both the OLD root and the NEW root of the rotated subtree need their heights recomputed, and the order matters, the old root (now a child) must be updated BEFORE the new root, since the new root's height computation depends on it.
Checking the balance factor before updating height: this reads stale height data and can miss a genuine imbalance or falsely trigger a rotation that was not actually needed.

Mishandling the Left Right and Right Left double rotation cases by only doing a single rotation: a single rotation on these cases does not fully restore balance, it is a well known trap to test the double rotation logic explicitly against a case designed to trigger it, not just the simpler single rotation cases.

Balance a Binary Search Tree: given an existing, possibly unbalanced BST, rebalance it, commonly solved by an inorder traversal to extract sorted values, then rebuilding a balanced tree from that sorted array, a different technique than AVL's incremental rotation approach.

Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree: a related but distinct construction problem, building a height balanced BST directly from a sorted array by always picking the middle element as the root, recursively, which naturally produces balance without any rotation logic at all.
